p:
Well, one area of focus for us is interagency coordination and being able to work across the various New York City agencies to identify vulnerable or more vulnerable clients. So just yesterday, I had the opportunity to talk with our new DOHMH Commissioner, as well as

representatives from New York City Health + Hospitals, Dr. Ted Long. And we're working on a partnership program where we can identify some of these socially isolated older New Yorkers. An additional enhancement at New York City Aging is that we are including flags in our system that will be able to flag for us any critical and at-risk older New Yorkers so that we can prioritize their needs in a more efficient manner.
Do we already have a senior agency task force with members from different agencies? I saw we...
Yes...
already have that one. But I don’t know what the activity has been so far.

Right. It’s the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers. And it is something that we feel has been very effectively coordinated, some of the services. But there are targeted needs, too, where you may need to have a subcommittee, or a sub ad hoc group, looking at specific issues.

So, absolutely, the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers will continue. And that’s something that we hope to have back up and running in the next few weeks. So you will have more information at that time.
So, there's no meeting, any meeting scheduled currently?

There are meetings scheduled, but I don’t have the date now. Perhaps one of my associates will hand me the date. But we do have meetings scheduled, and we are continuing the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers.

I see the bill, Preconsidered--I feel like if the Cabinet is already working on those issues, we would not need this bill in New York City. But because I feel there's a lack of communication, maybe internally, between the agencies, that's the reason our City Council Members have to introduce a bill to make sure different agencies work together to make sure the isolated adults get to be taken care of during extreme weather.

Well, this may be, you know, and obviously, you have the right

to your opinion on that, but I can tell you that I am aware that we have strong interagency collaboration. The Cabinet of Older New Yorkers just reinforces what's already happening at most of our agencies across the city. You can never have too much attention to an issue or concern for our older New Yorkers. So if we feel that, in addition to that, we need to stand up other bodies to look at these issues, we will certainly do that so that we have a real targeted approach to being able to address the needs of our older New Yorkers. And I just want to also circle back and say the Cabinet for older New Yorkers does meet quarterly, so we will be meeting shortly.

Do you think we can make that monthly instead of quarterly? We have a lot of issues about seniors, about housing, food, and isolation. It's not only just one agency's work, but it's multi-agency work to help our seniors.
It is.
If it meets quarterly, I don't think it's frequent enough to address those issues.

Well, that would be true if we weren't working on our own. You know, none of those agencies stopped working and waited for the quarter. So you know they are working independently, and usually at those meetings, they will come and provide updates as to what they're handling. So I absolutely agree. If it were quarterly only, you are right, that would not be frequent enough. So we do encourage them to continue to work, and as they come to those meetings, they bring very robust updates, which really let us know that they've continued working when those meetings are not being held.
Maybe this question should not be for the Commissioner of Aging, but for other commissioners. Will they have particular liaisons signed to senior-related issues?

Yes, they do, and I will say to you, and of course, you know, the other commissioners are just as focused as I am on New York City as a whole. Obviously, New York City Aging is more targeted to senior issues, but our

seniors are not forgotten in any of our New York City agencies.
Are we able to have a contact list so we can share it with council members, so when they have issues, they can go directly to those people?
Yeah, that would be a great idea.

Thank you. We're looking forward to having the list. Also, to follow up with Council Member Aldebol’s question about the winter social isolation, she talked about the NYCHA building; this winter and last winter, we have experienced extremely cold weather. A lot of seniors came to testify in the other hearing, not in this one, to talk about how it is very hard for them to get out of their homes. And then at the same time, does the NYC Aging coordinate with, like, winter awareness or get set up with an initiative so that social isolation among older adults-- they are able to have any virtual social engagement programs?

So between January 22nd and February 6th, our case

management and caregiver providers made approximately 16,400 wellness calls to ensure that some of our most vulnerable individuals were prepared for the storm. And 36 of those clients who were contacted received some direct support, such as additional food or meals, heating assistance, or over the counter medicine. New York City Aging amplified the cold weather alerts, and they use Notify NYC messages and Advanced Warning System notifications to the agency's service provider network, including all our contracted congregate, social, and direct care organizations.

Thank you, and I just want to also mention that, extreme weather, extreme heat, whatever may impact our older New Yorkers, we have a very robust and dynamic emergency preparedness program at New York City Aging. And I would also like to point to my previous work in Emergency Management, and I am a certified emergency manager. So it's always a focal point for us at the agency, making sure that we proactively prepare our older New Yorkers because we don't want to wait for something to happen, we want to make sure that they're always prepared, and if something does

happen, as a surprise, that at least we have the resources to roll out to assist them.

Thank you, Commissioner. I think your experience in emergency management will probably bring a lot of benefits this summer. If we have the same hot weather, you can help a lot of seniors in our city. Also, I would like to acknowledge that we have been joined by Chair Mealy. Chair Mealy, do you have some questions?

Yes, it's gonna be very brief. Sorry for being late. I have two meetings at the same time in the community. All the leaders are in the district. But I felt this was much more important. And I want to thank you, Dr. Scott-McKenzie, for the meeting. I'm looking forward to working with you so much more. And I want to just highlight, from the last hearing, I was able to put in my budget about $10,000 to give to (INAUDIBLE) Kcs Corona Older Adult Center to see how we could coordinate together, with transportation to bring in the seniors from there to Brooklyn. And I don't know how I'm going to do it to Brooklyn to Queens yet, but

I'm still looking to make sure that the isolation is not so intense that seniors withdraw and they almost give up. So I just want to tell you that. I have two questions, but I have to tell you something else. We just had the first Spades tournament in Brevard Houses, and it went to 9:00 P.M. I'm not going to tell you the organization because I got to work with them a little bit more, but how can we keep the senior centers open a little later? That was phenomenal. I brought my Spades partner. There were at least about 40 people in there, and that's how we keep our seniors--I'm not calling them seniors, my young seniors (LAUGHS) from isolation. But what was so good was that they gave us lunch—well, dinner. We stopped at 7:30, ate for 15 minutes, and started the tournament again. I only lost one game. But it still-- I'm going take it over soon. (LAUGHTER)

Don’t forget I do it every Friday, like today, at Mount Ararat, we have the Senior Center. Friday is usually my day off. I go there and play every Friday. (TIMER) Oh, can I? I

didn't even ask my question. Sorry. But please, we have to do more about the transportation. But thank you, we got to talk more on that to make sure that Staten Island, Queens, and Manhattan, we should be inter-agency and inter-senior centers networking with each other, because I found out, Urban Upbound, we were telling our seniors about the $790-- no $198.00 with your taxes. Seniors could automatically get that off the back. And that's been going on in my office for the last three months. You could be 99 years old,-–A lot of seniors leave that money on the table, so. The Director, Bishop Taylor, said that he plays Spades, so I want to pop up with him to go to the senior centers. And one thing I want to note is that it makes our seniors dress up a little more. They look forward to coming out, even at night. Everyone is not, you know, privy to coming out, but it's important for the ones that can. Let's get them out. What is NYC Aging doing to increase older adult access to transportation? Because if we had a bus to take people home or at least close by, we could have everyone out at night. And what coordination exists between the NYC Aging, DOT, and

MTA regarding Access-A-Ride to address transportation-related isolations? And what coordination exists between NYC Aging, DOT, and MTA Access-A-Ride to address transportation-related isolation (sic)? And I have to give it to Access-A-Ride, I've been talking to the seniors, we used to call it stress-a-ride. So now it's getting kind of light. They said, "No, I’m okay.” I guess the new cars are coming in, also, and not just the truck. So that's a plus. So how can we do that with transportation? Have y'all had any communication or collaboration?
So (LAUGHS)...
(LAUGHS) Sorry.
Thank you so much for your robust support and advocacy.
No, thank you.

CM Mealy. Thank you for our conversations regarding the sites that are within your district as well. And I just want to mention a few things. First off, we have been looking at whether or not there would be a way for us to keep some of the

centers open a little more in the summertime. In relation to our cooling centers as well. So that we pretty much kill two birds with one stone. So it is something that we are looking at right now. I'll also say that we do have an RFP coming out for both the OACs, as you know, to increase access, but also for transportation later on in the year. So there will be some opportunities to review the network.

Could you explain what kind of transportation? That we could be kind of clear, will it be taking seniors home or just to their Senior Center? Please, kind of-- could you kind of be direct? I wanna see where I could fit in if we don't have access for them to go directly back home or...
I'm not going to get into the weeds on that only because we know the RFP process is a competitive process and there'll be a lot... (CROSS-TALK)
But, it’s in there?

There are things that are in there that, once the RFP comes

out, it would be better to review them and then see where you fit in. So, I really don’t want to intervene too much in that process, so that it remains fair and equitable to all. Access-A-Ride is a state-run program, so there's not much that we can say about that right now. But I will say that we have written three letters to MTA advocating for Access-A-Ride for older adults. So that should be helpful. And as you know, there is a citywide focus--you know, our mayor has been very vocal about fast and free bus service and other things that would assist not just all New Yorkers, but definitely our older New Yorkers who oftentimes prefer to use bus service as opposed to subway service. So there are some opportunities there. And then lastly. I'll say on the issue of playing Spades. (LAUGHS) (LAUGHTER)
I might have to join you one day. I haven't played for a while.
We have a place for Mahjong from 2:00 to 5:00.
Oh, wonderful.
It’s at a community restaurant. So, anybody who plays Mahjong, please call my office. I need more... So, thank you so much.
(LAUGHS)
So, thank you so much.
Thank you.

Thank you. I also want to ask questions about digital-related and technical topics. How many older adult centers have implemented the digital literacy program required under Local Law 82 of 2023, and what metrics does NYC Aging use to evaluate whether it's reducing other forms of isolation?

Well, as you know, it is a focus area for us to try to increase the use of technology where possible, because it does help to connect older New Yorkers with the rest of the world and really helps to combat social isolation and loneliness.

But we do have some data on that, too. We know that technology access varies across the boroughs. For computer ownership with internet, our residents ranked highest to lowest, Manhattan at 73.1%, Staten Island at 71.9%, Brooklyn at 67.7%, the Bronx at 67.3%, and Queens at 61.3%. And there are also variations in home internet availability by age. But overall, New York City Aging's OACs and other services are able to stand in where there's a lack of internet access. As always, we know that those who are marginalized and underserved communities, historically disadvantaged groups may have less access, so this is an area of concern that I think the Council's partnership and citywide partnership will be needed.
Why is Queens only 61%? Do you know what the reason is that they are much lower?

No, I don't know what the reason is that they're much lower, but it could be something that we should look into. I would imagine that it does have something to do with what we've mentioned earlier, that some of these

communities are more marginalized and experience higher rates of poverty, and may not have internet access based on that.

There’s a joke I always make with my Asian colleagues: I said Queens has the largest Asian population, but Brooklyn has the largest Chinese population. That means, I believe Queens has more language access needs. Probably that's one of the reasons. I don't have the data, but this is what I feel. Maybe that's one of the reasons, because there's very limited language access. Even in Brooklyn, we have a large Asian population, but the majority is Chinese; Queens is very different. Queens has Korean, Thai, Filipino, like everyone from Asia, but in Brooklyn, there are more concentrated Chinese-speaking communities. Do you guys know any plans for language-related advertising online? I recently saw a lot of advertising about immigration in Chinese , but on Facebook. Chinese people, in general, especially those who only read Chinese, don't go to Facebook. Usually, they go to WeChat, but there's no advertising on WeChat, the platform.

That is one example of minority groups. Even though they have access to the internet for internet literacy, they still don't get the information because its advertising is on the wrong platform. This is the issue, there I see. I haven't seen any advertising for senior literacy on Facebook in different languages because I read Chinese, too. But I do not see that in Chinese-speaking seniors, the platform they usually use is a WeChat group. I would like to have the Administration do more research about different platforms. I know Koreans use a different platform, and Latinos use a different platform. Every culturally (INAUDIBLE) group uses different platforms. But for our city, everything is on Facebook or Instagram, which doesn't really serve the purpose there.

It's a great point, and we would welcome additional partnership with the Council on this issue because obviously, if we could increase the use of technology to assist or facilitate some of these language barriers, it would help our older adults as well. So definitely this is

an area that I think that we can join forces on to be sure that we are representing all and including all.

Yeah, I see a lot of senior centers, especially in my districts, that have language access that helps seniors and also serves the seniors. Even my Jewish senior center has people who speak Chinese to serve the Chinese community, and also speak Russian and Spanish. They serve everyone. I'm very proud of the service they provide, and I appreciate the work NYC Aging does in our community. But I just feel that the literacy in different languages is not published on their platform, say for like Russian-speaking seniors, the radio station they always hear--they told me 620 radio station, and the Chinese they don't hear, they don't go to Facebook, but the advertising is on Facebook. So, even (INAUDIBLE) language has language access, but it's not really putting the platform for that group of people. I think there's more work to be done over there. And what steps is NYC Aging taking to support immigrant older adults who report that the programs are not linguistically accessible and culturally appropriate?

Well, at every one of our centers, first of all, there is no focus on any one group. We welcome all. Anyone who's 60 and over can report to our centers, and we do provide culturally sensitive programming at every one of the sites. So if an older New Yorker does present and does not speak English, we can communicate with them at the center in their local community.

Thank you. Is there any research you guys are doing related to the community, what language they speak, what senior center they attend, and what languages they are able to provide? Like, say, my neighborhood, the majority speak Russian, Chinese, and Spanish. My neighborhood did a pretty good job, but how about the other neighborhoods? Do we have data to show any requirement for those senior centers?

I can't comment on senior centers, but I can say that generally when we have our RFPs, we do share information in terms of language and culture for particular areas so that the providers that are

applying are aware and can demonstrate how they'll serve those populations.

And I'd like to bring you back. I know that we do have information, because it has been included in our previous RFPs, uh, which languages in the particular communities that we have OACs. So we'll bring you some additional information on that, because it is a focus area for us, and always a concern that we are being very sensitive to the cultures that are represented in every community we serve.

Thank you. We are joined by Council Member Encarnación. She has a statement to make. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Hello, everyone. Thank you, Chair, for recognizing me. And I know you were kind of going down a road, which I actually approve of. As many of you know, I'm introducing a piece of legislation today. I'm also part of the Public Housing Committee, which is right next door, so I had to run over. I'll make this brief, but I did want to take the moment to talk about this piece of

legislation around extreme weather emergencies, especially since we've experienced so many this past winter. And knowing that they pose a clear and urgent threat to some of our most vulnerable members of the community, our older adults. For many of our seniors, these conditions are not merely uncomfortable; they're life-threatening. Seniors, particularly those who live alone or have limited mobility, are more likely to experience chronic health conditions, social isolation, and barriers to accessing timely assistance. So during these emergencies, these challenges are compounded, leaving too many without the ability to seek relief, access critical resources, or respond quickly to rapidly changing conditions. This is precisely why it's necessary that we introduce this legislation now. And this legislation represents a proactive, compassionate approach to safeguarding the health and dignity of those who would otherwise slip through the cracks in our city services. By establishing regular wellness checks for seniors living alone or exclusively with other seniors, we empower city agencies to prevent tragedy

before it occurs. These check-ins help older adults maintain their independence while ensuring that they remain connected to essential services and support systems. At the same time, the initiative equips NYC Aging, I hope, with the tools to better identify and monitor individuals at risk of social isolation, declining mental health, or deteriorating physical health. With improved data collection and coordination, NYC Aging will be better positioned to deliver targeted, timely services to those who need them the most. Again, I want to thank the Chair for allowing me to introduce this today and to thank the Speaker also for entrusting me with getting this across the finish line. And for everyone who will hopefully sign on to this piece of legislation and get us there, thank you.
Thank you. We have some questions following the statement. Does NYC Aging support this legislation?
As mentioned in my earlier testimony, we do align with the spirit of this introduction.
Do providers maintain standard operating procedures for outreach to older adults during code red and blue alerts? If so, what are they?

Absolutely. We have many different areas in which we interact with our older New Yorkers to make sure that they're in good condition during these types of events. And as mentioned earlier, we did perform 16,400 wellness checks during that critical period, where we did have the extreme cold last year. So, in addition to that, we do have our case management services, and we have our case managers who check on their clients. We have our home-delivered meals program, where you have that interaction on a daily basis during emergency events. And this is an area that we are also looking to expand, because one of the things that we noticed during the extreme cold was that you have our homebound older New Yorkers who are served through the delivery process. But then some of the sites weren't accessible because of the fact that it was so cold and that, you know, the snow was piled high and,

you know, folks were concerned about ambulating or being out walking around in that. So we also want to include a provision where we can look at where we have these types of issues. And I want to commend you, Chair, at one of your sites, they also mentioned that the providers there actually got into their private vehicles and made sure they went out and checked on the seniors who were not able to get to the OAC. But we want to have more of a structured approach from New York City Aging, so that we too can get to those older adults who maybe cannot access during cold weather. So in addition to that, we have the Friendly Visiting Program, our caregiving program, and I'm sure most of you have seen our really great caregiver campaign that has rolled out across the city, as well as Aging Connect. In Aging Connect, we will also have messaging proactively to advise older adults of where we have warming centers or other supports that they can access.

Thank you. Also, from experience, I believe you worked well.

What coordination currently exists between DFTA and New York City Emergency Management during extreme weather events?

We are very, very strong partners, as you know, we did partner not only with NYCEM, but also with all of the other city agencies to ensure that older adults have everything that they need to be able to navigate through any extreme weather event or any impacts that may be due to an emergency management situation in New York City.
Is there any particular person who will sign on to these types of events, in, I mean, in DFTA, probably yes, but in the City Emergency Management, especially for seniors?

Absolutely, because you would activate a citywide command center if we did have an event like that. And every one of our agencies has a liaison who would address Emergency Management for all New Yorkers, and specifically also for older adults.
What changes has DFTA made to protocol following the recent heat waves, the recent cold snap, or snowstorms?

Well, I've had the opportunity to review our programs, and as I mentioned, one change is that we do want to have a more robust approach to making sure that we can get meals to older adults who attend the OACS, not just the home-delivered meals program, but also, if there are any supports that are needed for that program to do that. And also, we are proactively preparing right now for the heating season. So one thing we've done already is we've activated a pre-season checklist where we're looking at each one of our sites, and we've had our provider network report to us on where they are with preparedness for heat in the summertime. We have a 96% response rate right now. And over the next week or so, we'll be focusing on that 4%, because I suspect that they may need some additional support, and those will be the focal areas for us at this time.

Thank you. In my district, we had a nonprofit donate 200 meals right before the storm. Extremely cold. We had close to 250 people show up who wanted a meal, and we didn’t have

enough. That shows the city has a strong need, especially before those storms. Do you have any plans for the summer when it's so hot, but people have to wait outside to get their meal?

We’re operating cooling centers throughout the city. So, this hopefully will not impact our older adults in New York City because we expect them to be inside at the cooling center. But, certainly, we are always partnering with the Council in relation to food insecurity, and we certainly want to make sure that anyone who needs a meal, who qualifies, 60 or older, that NYC Aging is responding to that need.

Because the issue I see is, like say for a food pantry in my district, no matter how hot or how cold it is, it always has at least 200 people waiting in line, no matter what food they give, the food insecurity is definitely the big issue. If they don't have enough food, no matter how cold or how hot the weather is, they always wait outside and wait in line.

We did the food pantry last year, and close to 100°, I was outside for three hours with my volunteers, and still, people waited. The food pantry starts at 11:00, and people start lining up at 7:00. And if the weather is extremely hot, I really worry about the majority being seniors, uh, people at risk. The city (INAUDIBLE), and how do we help? Are we able to provide food directly inside the cooling center? Probably, this is something we should consider together.

Definitely, we should work on this together. But I will give you my opinion as an emergency manager, there really is no reason for us to wait for the hottest period of the day to distribute meals. It could be done at a cooler period of the day. So you could potentially hand out the meals a little earlier than noon. You know, when we know that it's going to be sweltering, and you know, folks are standing out there, there could be a way to do that. So that would be my opinion as an emergency manager. But definitely, we welcome the partnership.
I think that's good advice. We'll talk to the nonprofits, see if they can actually do that, and it will be helpful. Thank you. Chair Mealy has more questions.

Yes, thank you. I just have one really-- Oh, and to piggyback on food insecurity, I think that something must be done to give more CBOs, more money to make sure that-- I have in my district, they come at 6:00-7:00 a.m. from Queens. Because (INAUDIBLE) rescue mission gives chicken, turkeys, meatloaf, everything, and they have it down to a science, a different program. So, I am going to learn their program and see if we can do it at every center. But they should not be waiting that long in line. One other thing I’ve got to ask is, food insecurity, why do seniors still have to pay to get lunch, even breakfast, $2.00 or $3.00, still have issues, a senior center just went to an event, and I know I gave about $50,000, and they had to pay $125.00 to go on this event--bus ride, for the senior center. Something has to change with that. But my question is, does NYC-- Oh, and I was doing an interview, and one of the seniors

brought it up. That kicked me under the bus. But I asked them why they had to pay $125.00 to go to Ace in the Hole or something like that. I never heard of it, but I want to attend one day. Does NYC Aging track how many older adults stop attending programs due to mobility decline, fear of falling, or lack of access to accessible transportation? If not, what would be the barrier to tracking such information? (TIMER)

Well, thank you again for your questions, Council Member Mealy. We did address the issues of mobility a little earlier in our testimony and also in our interaction here. And again, it's not something that we directly track, but we did share the information that we have on that. There's no barrier to following up with our older adults, the ones that are known to us, regarding their mobility issues, and certainly, it's something that we would welcome a partnership with you on. So, thank you for bringing that up again. I also want to talk about the issue of the wait time because, again, I just want to clarify that folks are not waiting that long for New York

City Aging meals. These are food pantries that you are referring to, which fall outside of our ages. But again, we welcome a partnership with you. If any of our older adults are being impacted by this, certainly it’s something that we want to ensure that they don't have to experience. So we welcome that. And lastly, on the issue of the suggested donation, and I know we spoke about this privately, we've spoken about this at the last hearing, and certainly glad to hear that, you know, it's something that you hold close to your heart, and you will continue to work on. On our part, though, we're at the point where that suggested donation, certainly, no older adult in the city is required to pay anything for any of the meals that are offered by NYC Aging. However, there is a rule for a suggested donation. Now, what we've looked at, obviously, you know, we've been out in the community, and we're visiting all of the older adult centers. And what we've noticed is perhaps sometimes the placement of that sign that speaks to the suggested donation may be in a place that's too conspicuous, because we don't want any older adult to be discouraged from

attending or thinking that others will notice if they donate or they don't donate. So that's what we're looking at right now, just to ensure that folks understand that this is a welcoming environment, that they're able to get a meal without giving anything. However, there is a suggested donation, and if they're willing to give something, they can.
Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. And let's go to mental health issues. How many older adults were referred to mental health services through the older adult centers, case management agencies, or NYC Wellness in the last fiscal year, compared to the last three fiscal years?
So we generally don't track where older adults are referred from. And overall, in FY25, the Geriatric Mental Health program served 6,594 older adults, with 1,419 receiving clinical services.

So there's no way to know which seniors-- because I went to a couple of senior centers. The provider worked there-- and the senior actually told me, they did not know they

needed mental health services, and if the service is on-site, seniors feel more comfortable going to those services. I also talked to one of my colleagues about the homeless issue, especially for older adults. The homeless issue, a lot of us are out on the streets, and we talk to people who are homeless. A lot of the time, they have a home. They have a family. Actually, their family brings the meal to where they choose to be homeless. And a lot of the time, those people are affected by mental health issues. And then we try to help get those people back home. They don't want to. But the mental health issue, if not addressed in their senior center, or where they often may go, they will never choose the service. Because no one wants to tell people, “I have a mental health issue.” If I need help with mental health issues, I probably don't want to tell people, either. They feel embarrassed. If we have those mental health services in the centers or wherever the seniors go to hang out, it will probably serve them better. One of the senior center mental service program people told me, “We go where they go. We

serve them where they are, not so they have to come to find us.” That will be more effective. I would like to see how many senior centers have this type of service.

And we can give you the numbers on that because we do have licensed clinicians that are placed in our centers just for that reason. We don't want any older adult to be stigmatized or to feel as if they have-- they're embarrassed to seek services.
Yeah.
So we come to where they are, we meet them where they are, to be sure that we can offer the services to our older adults.
Yeah. We just like to know what percentage of senior centers offer this type of service.
Absolutely, and we will provide that for you.

Okay, thank you. How is NYC Aging integrating social isolation screening into case management assessment?

(INAUDIBLE) go back to senior centers again, friendly visits or wellness checks?

So as part of the case management assessment, they assess for loneliness and social isolation. And if a client is lonely, socially isolated, one of the resources they can refer to is our Friendly Visiting program. Our Friendly Visiting program also assesses for loneliness and social isolation, and when a client is matched with a volunteer, they repeat that assessment again six months later to see where there's improvement.

And how many older adults are comfortable using a hotline or digital platforms? How is NYC Aging investing in literacy access, mental health services in adult senior centers, NORCS, or home-based programs?

So, a few things — I just want to go back one moment and just mention again that we are always seeking additional volunteers for our Friendly Visiting Program. And as I noted before, folks who would like to assist in this process can call us at Aging Connect 212-Aging NYC or 212-244-6469.

We have shortages in areas, particularly in the South Bronx, where we could use additional assistance. So I want to talk about... (CROSS-TALK)
Say that number again?
How many phone calls do you guys receive?

Well, we received approximately 800 or so calls to our Aging Connect program every day, excuse me, over the month. So we do have folks that are calling in to seek additional supports, and we provide those supports to the folks who have called in for assistance. There's always more work to be done on really getting more data as to how many of our older New Yorkers actually require these services. So it is a focal area for us, and we would like to present more data in the future on that as well.
How many people work to receive those 800 phone calls every month?
Excuse me, I have to go back-- it's 800 a week... (CROSS-TALK)
Eight hundred a week
for those calls. Uh...
How many people work there do we have...

We have seven... Seven fulltime workers are there right now. And we are looking at those seven fulltime, because we actually want to expand the hours for Aging Connect. So that is something that we will bring you more information on as well. Because we really feel as if we would like to have more service hours available--live persons, as opposed to providing an answer service, which we do have later on, along with messaging after hours and on weekends.
So if there's a person who needs language support, are they still able to call this phone number?

They can call that number 24/7. Our preference would be to have live persons as much as possible. So that's where we're putting the emphasis at this point. But

they can call 24/7. They will get information on how they can move forward with whatever needs they have.
Okay. Thank you. And, for language access, can they be in any language?

Well, there are many languages that are known to us, and we do have a language bank as well. So far, we haven't identified any languages that we haven't been able to meet. So I would say it's multilingual at this point. And if there's a need to add additional languages, then we can do that as well.
Thank you. And how does NYC Aging evaluate whether Friendly Visits, home-delivered meals, and case management are efficiently reducing isolation rather than simply providing a service touchpoint?

As I mentioned, there's an assessment that the case management agency does to assess for loneliness and isolation, and then based on the needs of the client, they could be referred to our Friendly Visiting Program. Again, there's another assessment that's done there. And they'll reassess after six months of

a continuous match with a volunteer to see where there is improvement.
Are adult centers required to conduct wellness checks? And then what do they do during holidays?

Yes, they do. They are required to conduct wellness checks. During holidays, they do make sure that they have proactively assessed any of our older adults who may have needs, and those needs are referred back to New York City Aging, and we make sure that they're met.
What gaps have been identified by NYC Aging providers regarding isolation during winter months, and how is NYC Aging addressing them?

Well, as we mentioned earlier, there are some gaps. And one of the gaps that we are trying to work on now has to do with the delivery of the meals, as I mentioned during inclement weather, and some of the barriers that were faced across the entire city, but also a more pronounced issue in our older New Yorkers. So we’re working to enhance that network to be sure that we're able to get to our older New

Yorkers when there is an issue, and also again, proactively preparing them when we have advanced notice of an event so that they are prepared to continue their daily living.

Of the more than 200,000 older adults served by NYC Aging and its providers in FY 2024, how many received no ongoing relationship-based services, such as Friendly Visit support groups, and instead have only transactional or one-time intentions-- one-time interaction?

So I can comment on Friendly Visiting. Approximately 1,200 unduplicated clients were served as part of that program, and these are clients who are also part of the case management program. Some of your other questions, I feel like we have to get back to.

So, how many received no ongoing relationship-based services, and they instead have only one-time interaction? Some people just have one-time interactions. Sometimes people have ongoing, every single day, someone goes there to deliver a meal.

Well, we aren't tracking how many come just for one meal. But

I would say we would rather focus on having that one meal when they need it. So, ensuring that we have access, open access to anyone who qualifies for a meal, I think, for New York City Aging is more of a focal point. And then our older adults have the right to choose. You know, perhaps, they may come in for one meal, and they may decide that they want to go to another site, or they may decide that they would prefer to have their meals at home. So it's difficult to track those who are moving because of preference.
Do we have a percentage number, like what is the percentage of people who have ongoing service, and what’s the percentage of people who only have one-time service?
As my associate mentioned, we will have to try to dig into the numbers and bring them back, if that’s available.

Okay. Let's go to a Council Member Lee's bill. Does NYC Aging support this legislation-- uh, Council Member Lee’s legislation, requiring the Department of Aging to maintain non-digital access to forms and services?

As mentioned earlier, yes, we do support the intent of this

introduction. Any bill that would make it easier for our older adults to access services, we will actively support.
Can you describe the current extent to which NYC Aging services and forms are only accessible online? Do you have anything only accessible online, not on paper?

Not to my knowledge. Again, we will perform another assessment, but we typically try to make forms available in as many modalities as possible. And as you know, we have a very robust network of navigators and folks who will assist older New Yorkers to be able to prepare and complete forms. So oftentimes that's also on paper. So, I would say at this point that we're making every effort to make sure that, whether it's online or in paper, our older adults are able to access services.
What outreach strategy does NYC Aging and its partners use to ensure older adults know they can access services without using the internet?

While at our OACS, we do emphasize the fact that our older adults

can be assisted without internet service to be able to complete and access any forms or services. So it is something that we actively, as I mentioned earlier, support, and we'll continue to do so.
Thank you, Commissioner. Do you have more questions? Okay, I’ve asked all the questions I wanted to ask. Thank you so much.
Thank you.

Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Gayle Horowitz, and I'm the CEO of JASA. Addressing social isolation requires strengthening the infrastructure of connection across

the entire aging services system. OACs, NORC programs, and affordable senior housing are among the City's most effective tools to combat isolation. They provide routine, accessible opportunities for connection, engagement, and support, and they work because they are place-based, consistent, and trusted, but they require greater flexibility and investment to serve a diverse and growing older adult population. Affordable senior housing in particular plays a dual role, addressing the housing crisis while combating isolation. At our sites, we foster vibrant, connected communities that support successful aging in place. Through our residential services programs, 1,089 residents received benefits last year-- benefits assistance, 577 received home visits, and 533 people received housing stability assistance. Initiatives like New York City Aging's Pop-up Cafe show that combining meals, programming, and social engagement within senior housing can significantly reduce isolation, especially for those with mobility challenges. And investing in affordable

housing is cost effective, reducing the need for premature and costly nursing home placement. (TIMER) I just have a little bit more. At the same time, many of the most isolated older adults never walk through the doors of an OAC or NORCS, nor live in affordable housing. To reach them, JASA launched JASAChat, pairing volunteers with clients for weekly calls — 98% of participants reported improved well-being. We've also launched JASACakes, because too many older adults spend their birthdays alone. Every home-delivered client, nearly 2,700 people, will receive a birthday celebration this year. Outreach must be funded as essential infrastructure, not an add-on. And my last topic — Social isolation is closely linked to depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline. At JASA, meaningful engagement is often the first step toward improved mental health. Our geriatric mental health clinic provided 5,000 hours of services last year, but we could reach so many more. Programs that embed mental health services within OACs and community settings are particularly effective because they reduce stigma and meet people where they are.

The City should expand investment in these integrated models. Social isolation is preventable, but only with intentional investment and outreach, flexible community-based models, and integrated mental health services. Thank you.

Chairperson Zhuang and Members of the Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today. My name is Mark Meridy, and I'm the Executive Director of DOROT in Manhattan. DOROT was founded 50 years ago with the mission of alleviating social isolation and loneliness among older adults. We're unique among nonprofits in that building meaningful social connections, thereby easing social isolation and loneliness, is not simply part of what we do—it's built into everything we do. Every program we offer is designed to help older adults build social connections with others and to feel a sense of purpose and belonging.

The challenge is that social connection is an underappreciated factor in one's overall health and well-being, and that's despite the fact that feeling socially connected, regardless of one’s age, helps us thrive even when faced with other physical and emotional challenges. What we've learned at DOROT is that there are many effective ways to build meaningful social connections. This includes programming that is in person or conducted virtually or over the telephone. Regardless of the modality, the unifying factor in all of our programming is that we are highly intentional and focused on building meaningful connections, and we know that we are making a profound difference. However, there is simply not enough attention paid at the city, state, or federal levels to the importance of an individual's social health and well-being. Therefore, it is imperative that the City create an effective strategy to build and support a stronger social infrastructure. The key to easing social isolation and loneliness is putting meaningful connections at the heart of as many programs as

possible and providing the resources and flexibility to reach people in a multitude of ways. I am grateful that the Committee on Aging is focused on easing social isolation among New York's older adults. We at DOROT are happy to assist in any way that we can. Thank you very much for the opportunity.
